items.summary: Design Kestrel's network zones and the flows allowed between them, decide where firewalls, intrusion detection and secure protocols act, and choose the logs the managed security operations centre needs, with rules for time, integrity and retention.

read.heading: Why a flat hospital network is dangerous
read.body:
Ransomware rarely starts on the system it encrypts. It lands on a workstation or a remote session, steals credentials, then moves sideways to the servers that matter. On a flat network, where every device can reach every other, that is easy. Segmentation splits the network into zones and allows only the flows each zone needs.

Kestrel's records show the risk. SEC-004, the Critical ransomware precursor of 2026-08-11, hit the Virtual Desktop Service (A-008), which is how clinicians reach the Clinical Information System (CIS, A-001) from shared workstations. The same service had malware in July (SEC-002) and September (SEC-008). And 12 of Kestrel's 15 systems depend directly on the Identity Directory (A-007) in khn_assets.csv, so an attacker who reaches it reaches almost everything.

Today you design the zones, the allowed flows and the logging that lets the security operations centre (SOC) see an attack in progress.

read.heading: Kestrel's zones and micro-segmentation
read.body:
In this lesson ED means emergency department, PACS is the Picture Archiving and Communication System and MFA is multi-factor authentication.

| Zone | What lives there | Main rule |
|---|---|---|
| Z1 Clinical core | CIS (A-001), ED Tracking Board (A-002), Laboratory (A-003), Pharmacy (A-005), Bed Management (A-006) | Users arrive only through the Z5 virtual desktops; interfaces between named servers only |
| Z2 Imaging | PACS (A-004) and imaging devices | Devices talk only to the systems they feed; no internet |
| Z3 Legacy quarantine | Clinical Paging (A-014), past end of support | Paging traffic only; nothing else in or out |
| Z4 Management and identity | Identity Directory (A-007), administrator jump hosts, log collector | Administrators only, with MFA |
| Z5 User access | Virtual Desktop Service (A-008) hosts | Clinician sessions after MFA and single sign-on |
| Z6 Workstations | Shared clinical workstations and staff devices | Untrusted by default; no direct route to Z1 |
| Z7 Analytics | Warehouse (A-010) and the on-premises data gateway | Scheduled extracts in; the gateway only opens outbound connections to the Power BI service |

Everything else is External: NorthArc Cloud (A-011, A-012, A-013, A-015), the Power BI service (A-009), Sentinel SOC Services (V-04) and vendor support. External parties reach Kestrel only through defined flows.

Between zones, a firewall or access control list applies default deny: everything is blocked and logged unless a documented flow allows it, with source, destination, port, reason and owner. Medical and imaging devices are isolated because manufacturers must validate patches first, so you protect them by isolation rather than fast patching. A-014 gets a quarantine zone for a stronger reason: it no longer receives security fixes at all.

Micro-segmentation applies policy per workload, often with host firewalls or software-defined networking. The CIS database accepts connections only from the CIS application servers, so a compromised server elsewhere in Z1, such as the Bed Management System, cannot reach it even though both sit in the same zone. That stops ransomware moving sideways inside a zone.

read.heading: Firewalls, VPN and zero trust network access
read.body:
Firewall types, with the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) layers they work at:

- Packet filter: stateless; checks addresses and ports (layers 3 and 4). Fast but blind to sessions.
- Stateful inspection: tracks connections and allows return traffic only for permitted sessions. The usual zone boundary control.
- Application-level proxy: understands the protocol at layer 7; slower but precise.
- Next-generation firewall: stateful inspection plus application awareness, user identity and intrusion prevention.
- Web application firewall: blocks attacks such as injection against web applications.

A virtual private network (VPN) builds an encrypted tunnel and usually places the signed-in user on the network, free to try whatever they can route to. Zero trust network access (ZTNA) brokers one application at a time, checks identity, MFA and device health every session, and never gives the user an address inside Kestrel. NIST Special Publication 800-207, from the National Institute of Standards and Technology, describes zero trust architecture.

Beacon's decision: Meridian (V-01) and NorthArc (V-02) support reach Kestrel only through a jump host in Z4, with MFA, a ticket approved by the system owner, a time limit and recording (flow FL-09). ZTNA is the stronger long-term option. The Meridian engineer, Raj Patel (E-015), shows why this matters: his enabled privileged account has no MFA and no end date, and holds an excess grant to view charts in the CIS.

read.heading: Where controls act: layers, IDS and IPS, secure protocols
read.body:
| Layer | Name | Example controls |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | Application | Web application firewall, email filtering, CIS audit logging |
| 4 | Transport | Stateful rules on TCP and UDP ports |
| 3 | Network | Routing, access control lists, IPsec tunnels |
| 2 | Data link | VLANs, 802.1X port authentication |
| 1 | Physical | Locked closets, disabled unused wall ports |

TCP and UDP are the Transmission Control Protocol and User Datagram Protocol, IPsec is Internet Protocol Security, and VLANs are virtual local area networks.

An intrusion detection system (IDS) watches a copy of traffic and alerts; it cannot block. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) sits inline and blocks, so a false positive stops legitimate traffic. Either can be network-based or host-based and detect by signature (known patterns) or anomaly (departure from a baseline, which catches new attacks but raises more false alarms). A wrongly blocked clinical interface is a patient-safety event, so Beacon runs new IPS rules in detect-only mode in front of clinical and device zones, tunes them, then blocks.

Secure protocol swaps: Telnet to Secure Shell (SSH); File Transfer Protocol to SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP); plain web traffic to Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) with Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2 or 1.3; Simple Network Management Protocol versions 1 and 2c to version 3; directory queries to Lightweight Directory Access Protocol over TLS (LDAPS). Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) prove name answers are genuine but do not encrypt them. Two weak cipher findings are open: SEC-013 on Email (A-013) and SEC-018 on IT Service Management (A-011).

read.heading: What the SOC needs to see
read.body:
Security information and event management (SIEM) collects logs, normalizes them, correlates events across sources, raises alerts and keeps records for investigation. Sentinel SOC Services (V-04) monitors Kestrel's SIEM; Sam Okafor (E-020) is the liaison.

| Log source | What it shows | Kestrel case |
|---|---|---|
| Identity Directory (A-007) | Sign-ins, failures, MFA, new accounts, privileged group changes | SEC-009 |
| Zone firewalls and the vendor jump host | Allowed and denied flows, vendor sessions | Movement from A-008 |
| Endpoint detection and response (EDR) | Processes, file changes, encryption behaviour | SEC-004 |
| Email security (A-013) | Phishing, malicious attachments | SEC-001, SEC-007, SEC-010 |
| Backup Platform (A-012) | Failed jobs, deletions, immutability changes | Attackers target backups first |
| CIS (A-001) audit log | Who opened which patient record | SEC-003 |
| Power BI activity log (A-009) | Exports, sharing, permission changes | SEC-006 |

Privacy shapes the design. Sentinel processes log data in the United States (risk R-05). No Alberta statute bans storage outside Canada, but section 60 of the Health Information Act (HIA) requires safeguards that protect health information stored or used outside Alberta. So Kestrel forwards security events only, replaces patient identifiers in CIS audit events with a pseudonymous token, and keeps the full CIS audit logs, which identify the patient record opened, in its own store in Canada. Priya Raman (E-003) owns R-05 and reviews the design and the contract safeguards.

read.heading: Time, integrity and retention
read.body:
Time: every device and the SIEM use the same internal Network Time Protocol (NTP) sources, and logs record Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) or the offset. SEC-008 shows contained_at at 13:10, before detected_at at 14:30 on 2026-09-09; until the SOC corrects it, the record is useless for timing.

Integrity: forward logs in near real time to the SIEM and to write-once storage, hash archived files so tampering shows, and separate duties so nobody administers the logs of systems they run. Today Kevin Park (E-009) provisions accounts, approves access and administers audit logs (issue I-01); Beacon moves log administration to security (E-020).

Retention: Kestrel policy sets the period for each log type. Beacon proposes 1 year for security logs and 10 years for CIS access logs, the period the provincial logging standard sets for Alberta electronic health record access logs. These are proposals; Priya Raman (E-003) and Daniel Osei (E-004) agree the final values.

keyTerms.definition: Dividing a network into zones of similar trust and allowing only documented flows between them, with a default deny rule for everything else.
Applying access policy per workload or server rather than per zone, so a compromised device cannot reach other systems even inside the same zone.
Access brokered to one application per session after checking identity, MFA and device health, without giving the user a network address inside the organization.
A passive monitor that inspects a copy of traffic or host activity and raises alerts. It cannot block traffic.
An inline control that detects and blocks malicious traffic. A false positive blocks legitimate traffic, so rules are tuned in detect mode first.
A platform that collects, normalizes and correlates logs from many sources, raises alerts and keeps records for investigation.
A firewall stance in which every flow is blocked unless a documented rule allows it, with a source, destination, port, reason and owner.

examTips.tip: Domain 4, Communication and Network Security: when a question asks how to limit the spread of ransomware, segmentation and micro-segmentation beat stronger passwords or more antivirus. An inline control that blocks is an IPS; a passive monitor that only alerts is an IDS.

Domain 4, Communication and Network Security: match controls to layers. VLANs and 802.1X work at layer 2, IPsec at layer 3, stateful port rules at layer 4, and web application firewalls and proxies at layer 7.

Domain 7, Security Operations (logging and monitoring): synchronized time is a precondition for correlation and for evidence. If logs disagree on time, fix NTP before you trust any timeline built from them.

pitfalls: Allowing any-to-any traffic between internal zones because a flow is hard to document. Every allowed flow needs a source, destination, port, reason and owner.
Switching a new IPS straight to block mode in front of clinical systems. A false positive that stops a clinical interface is a patient-safety event.
Sending CIS audit logs that identify patient records to a SOC that processes data in the United States without privacy review and contract safeguards (R-05).
Letting system administrators administer their own audit logs, which lets one person act and erase the evidence (I-01).

check.q: Why does Beacon micro-segment the CIS database even though it already sits in the clinical core zone (Z1)?
check.a: Zone rules control traffic between zones, not inside them. A compromised server elsewhere in Z1, such as the Bed Management System, could still reach the database. Micro-segmentation lets the database accept connections only from the CIS application servers, which stops ransomware moving sideways inside the zone.

check.q: What is the practical difference between a VPN and ZTNA for Meridian's support engineer?
check.a: A VPN usually places the engineer on Kestrel's network after sign-in, so they can try to reach anything routable. ZTNA brokers access to one named application per session, checks identity, MFA and device health each time, and never gives an address inside Kestrel. It also makes expiry and session recording simple.

check.q: SEC-008 shows contained_at before detected_at. Which logging control helps prevent this, and how is the record treated now?
check.a: Synchronized time: every device and the SIEM use the same NTP sources and record UTC or an offset, so timestamps line up. Until Sam Okafor (E-020) supplies the true times, SEC-008 stays in incident counts but is left out of every time measure.

items.summary: Build a consistent way to rate security incidents by severity, impact, urgency and priority, write a ransomware playbook from preparation to recovery, and connect incidents to problem management using Kestrel's real incident records.

read.heading: Severity, impact, urgency and priority
read.body:
Four words get mixed up in incident work. Keep them apart.

- Severity: how serious the security event is. Kestrel records Critical, High, Medium or Low in khn_security_events.csv.
- Impact: how much harm results: patient safety, number of sites and users, sensitivity of the data, legal consequences.
- Urgency: how fast the harm grows if nothing is done.
- Priority: the order in which work is done. In ITIL it comes from impact and urgency.

Kestrel's incident classification model uses severity as its impact measure and adds urgency (the incident is spreading, or a shift or clinic is about to start). It uses the service desk's priority codes so one queue works:

| Priority | Usually | Triage (proposed) | Containment started (proposed) | Service restored |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Critical, or High and spreading | 15 minutes | 1 hour | 4 hours |
| P2 | High | 30 minutes | 4 hours | 8 hours |
| P3 | Medium | 4 hours | 24 hours | 24 hours |
| P4 | Low | Next business day | 72 hours | 72 hours |

The restore column is the service desk's existing targets (sla_target_hours in the service desk data). For a security incident it means service back, perhaps with a workaround; full recovery is tracked separately. Severity criteria, patient safety first:

- Critical: a tier 1 clinical service down or at imminent risk at one or more sites, or Restricted health information encrypted, copied or destroyed at scale.
- High: a tier 1 system affected while care continues, a privileged account compromised, or confirmed unauthorized access to Restricted or Confidential data.
- Medium: a tier 2 or 3 system, or one tier 1 device, contained, with no confirmed access to Restricted data.
- Low: one user, no service impact, nothing exposed.

Two rules: the highest level any criterion reaches sets the severity, and when you are unsure you classify one level higher and lower it later with evidence. Privacy is assessed separately: any incident touching Restricted data goes to Priya Raman (E-003) whatever its severity. Kestrel's 10 unique incidents split Critical 1, High 3, Medium 4, Low 2.

read.heading: The incident response lifecycle
read.body:
The classic model is NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-61 Rev. 2 from the National Institute of Standards and Technology. It has four phases:

1. Preparation: policy, playbooks, trained people, contact lists, tools, tested backups.
2. Detection and analysis: spot the signs, confirm an incident, scope it, rate it, record it.
3. Containment, eradication and recovery: stop the spread, remove the cause, restore service and watch for return.
4. Post-incident activity: lessons learned, evidence retention and improvement actions.

The phases loop. Analysis often finds more affected systems, which sends you back to containment, and lessons learned feed preparation.

Rev. 3, published in April 2025, superseded Rev. 2. It frames incident response around the six Functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. Preparation now sits mostly in Govern, Identify and Protect, and response and recovery in Respond and Recover. Many teams and study guides still teach the four phases, so learn both. CISSP study material also often lists seven steps: detection, response, mitigation, reporting, recovery, remediation and lessons learned.

Kestrel's SEC-004 shows the lifecycle in real times: the activity began at 02:20 on 2026-08-11, was detected at 03:05, the record was opened at 03:20, containment came at 05:45, and normal service returned at 18:30 on 2026-08-13.

read.heading: Ransomware playbook: the first hours
read.body:
A playbook is a pre-agreed set of steps with an owner and a trigger for each. For ransomware, the first hours decide how bad the day becomes.

1. Declare. An endpoint detection and response (EDR) alert, a ransom note or locked files makes the service desk raise a P1 and call security. Daniel Osei (E-004) or his delegate becomes incident commander and declares a major incident.
2. Isolate, do not power off. Cut affected hosts from the network through EDR isolation, a switch port or a firewall rule, but leave them running. Powering off destroys memory evidence: running processes, network connections and sometimes keys.
3. Protect what recovery needs. Separate the Backup Platform (A-012) from production, end vendor remote sessions and confirm the immutable backup copy. CT-005 confirmed an immutable Clinical Information System (CIS) backup copy in NorthArc's Canadian region on 2026-09-24.
4. Contain identities. Disable compromised accounts and reset privileged credentials from a clean administrator workstation. The Identity Directory (A-007) is the attacker's prize, since 12 of 15 systems depend on it.
5. Preserve evidence: memory images, logs and a copy of the ransom note, under chain of custody.
6. Start clinical downtime. Chloe Dubois (E-016), Business Continuity Lead, activates downtime procedures for affected areas.

read.heading: Ransomware playbook: eradicate, recover, decide
read.body:
Eradication removes the attacker, not just the encryption. Find the entry point and every persistence mechanism, rebuild affected hosts from known-good images rather than cleaning them, close the weakness used, and reset all privileged and service account passwords.

Recovery restores from backups taken before the infection and scanned clean. Restore in the inventory order: the Identity Directory (A-007) first; then the Backup Platform (A-012) and Clinical Paging (A-014); then the Virtual Desktop Service (A-008) and the CIS (A-001); then A-002, A-003 and A-005; then tier 2 and tier 3. Clinical owners check the data before go-live, monitoring stays heightened for re-infection, and zones reconnect in stages.

Plan for the evidence you have. Both CIS restore tests failed: 9.0 hours and 13.5 hours against a 4-hour recovery time objective (RTO), and the last test was on 2025-08-14. The playbook must assume downtime procedures may run for more than half a day.

Paying a ransom is not an IT decision. It belongs to Kestrel's accountable executives, with legal counsel and law enforcement input and the Chief Information Security Officer's advice. Payment does not guarantee working decryption or the deletion of stolen data, and counsel must confirm whether a payment would be lawful. The playbook names the decision-makers in advance and lists the facts they need, above all how long recovery will take without paying.

read.heading: Incident, major incident, problem, known error
read.body:
ITIL keeps restoring service and removing causes apart.

- Incident: an unplanned interruption to a service or a reduction in its quality. Incident management restores normal service as fast as possible.
- Major incident: an incident with such high impact that it needs its own procedure: a dedicated lead, shorter timescales, frequent communication and a review afterwards. SEC-004 was Kestrel's major incident.
- Problem: the cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents. Problem management reduces how often incidents happen and how much harm they do.
- Known error: a problem that has been analyzed but not yet resolved.
- Workaround: a way to reduce or remove the impact of an incident or problem while a full fix is not available.

Patterns in the data call for problem records. The Virtual Desktop Service had SEC-002 (Medium malware, 2026-07-14), SEC-004 (Critical, 2026-08-11) and SEC-008 (Medium malware, 2026-09-09): three incidents on one tier 1 system in three months. Email (A-013) had three phishing incidents: SEC-001 (High), SEC-007 (Medium) and SEC-010 (Low). Each incident was closed, but the causes remain.

The workflow runs: incident logged, categorized and prioritized; diagnosed; resolved or worked around; closed. Trends and major incidents raise a problem; analysis finds the cause; a known error is recorded with its workaround; a change removes the cause; the problem closes once the fix is verified. Grace Liu (E-005) owns incident records, Sam Okafor (E-020) leads security analysis, and each problem gets a named owner. In ITIL's product and service lifecycle this work sits in the Operate and Support stages, and fixes return through Build and Transition as changes.

keyTerms.definition: The order in which incidents are worked, set from impact (how much harm) and urgency (how fast harm grows), not from who shouts loudest.
An incident with high impact that needs a separate procedure: a dedicated lead, shorter timescales, frequent communication and a formal review afterwards.
The cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents. Problem management finds and removes causes so incidents happen less often or do less harm.
A problem that has been analyzed but not yet resolved, usually recorded with a workaround so support teams can restore service quickly.
A way to reduce or remove the impact of an incident or problem while a full resolution is not yet available.
Actions that stop an incident spreading or causing more harm, such as isolating hosts and disabling accounts, while preserving evidence.
Removing the cause of an incident: the malware, the attacker's persistence and the weakness used, often by rebuilding from known-good images.

examTips.tip: Domain 7, Security Operations (incident management): know the NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 phases in order, and that Rev. 3 (April 2025) superseded it and frames response around the CSF 2.0 Functions. In ransomware questions, the first action is usually to contain by isolating affected systems, not to power them off, pay or restore at once.
Incident management restores service; problem management removes causes. A workaround restores service but does not close the problem, and a known error is a problem analyzed but not yet resolved.
Domain 1, Security and Risk Management: paying a ransom is a business decision for senior management with legal advice. The security professional gives facts and advice; they do not decide.

pitfalls: Powering off infected machines. It destroys memory evidence; isolate them from the network instead.
Restoring from the newest backup without proving it predates the infection, which can restore the attacker along with the data.
Closing the problem when the incident closes. Three malware incidents on A-008 need a problem record and a root cause even though each was restored.
Leaving the ransom decision to whoever is on call. The playbook names the executive and legal decision-makers in advance.

check.q: SEC-002, SEC-004 and SEC-008 all occurred on the Virtual Desktop Service. What ITIL record should this pattern create, and why?
check.a: A problem record, because a problem is the cause or potential cause of one or more incidents. Each incident was restored, but three malware incidents on one tier 1 system in three months suggest a shared cause. Problem management finds it, records a known error and workaround, and raises a change to remove it.

check.q: In the first hour of a suspected ransomware attack on a server, why isolate it rather than shut it down?
check.a: Isolation stops the spread while keeping volatile evidence such as running processes, network connections and memory contents, which may show how the attacker got in and sometimes hold keys. Shutting down loses that evidence and can trigger more damage on restart.

check.q: Name the four phases of NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 and say what changed with Rev. 3.
check.a: Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity. Rev. 3, published in April 2025, superseded Rev. 2 and frames incident response around the CSF 2.0 Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.

items.summary: Decide who is told about a security incident, by whom and how fast: internal escalation tiers, the Health Information Act breach duty for patient information, the Protection of Privacy Act test for staff information, communication roles, and evidence handling with chain of custody.

read.heading: Two laws, two tests
read.body:
Kestrel is a public body and a custodian under the Health Information Act (HIA). Patient health information falls under the HIA. Non-health personal information, such as staff records, falls under the Protection of Privacy Act (POPA), which does not apply to health information held by a public body that is an HIA custodian.

| Question | HIA: patient health information | POPA: staff and other non-health personal information |
|---|---|---|
| What triggers the duty | Loss of, or unauthorized access to or disclosure of, health information | Loss of, or unauthorized access to or disclosure of, personal information |
| The test | A risk of harm to an individual | A reasonable person would consider there is a real risk of significant harm |
| Who is notified | The Commissioner, the Minister responsible under the Act and the affected individuals | The affected individuals, the Commissioner and the Minister responsible under the Act |
| How fast | The Commissioner as soon as practicable | Without unreasonable delay |

The HIA test, risk of harm, is a lower bar than POPA's real risk of significant harm. Do not mix them up. Under section 60.1 of the HIA, an affiliate (employees, contractors, volunteers, students, agents and information managers) must tell the custodian about a breach. The custodian then notifies the Commissioner, the Minister responsible under the Act and the affected individuals. Notice to individuals is in writing. The factors for judging risk of harm are set in the Health Information Regulation. Kestrel may withhold notice to an individual if it could reasonably be expected to harm that person's mental or physical health, but must then tell the Commissioner. Failing to notify is an offence under the Act.

Under POPA, if the incident falls below the real risk of significant harm threshold, notice to the Commissioner and the Minister is not required. Kestrel policy still records every assessment and its reasoning, whichever law applies.

read.heading: Applying the tests to Kestrel's incidents
read.body:
Practise on real records from khn_security_events.csv. The data shows what happened to systems; the assessment needs facts the investigation must still supply.

- SEC-003, unauthorized access on the Clinical Information System (CIS, A-001). The CIS holds Restricted, individually identifying health information, so the HIA applies if records were viewed. The access began at 22:10 on 2026-07-29 and was detected at 10:15 on 2026-08-02, about 84 hours later, a long exposure window. Facts needed: which records, by whom, for what purpose. Given the lower HIA bar, plan for notice to the Commissioner, the Minister and each affected patient.
- SEC-009, unauthorized access on the Identity Directory (A-007). The directory holds staff account data, not health information, so POPA applies; if the attacker reached health information through it, the HIA applies too. Facts needed: which accounts and fields, whether passwords or other credentials were exposed. It is still Contained, not recovered.
- SEC-005, a lost device with access to Email (A-013). Was it encrypted? Was it wiped? Did the mailbox hold patient details? If patient health information was on it, the HIA test applies; if only staff information, POPA.
- SEC-006, a misconfiguration on Power BI (A-009). Beacon dashboards hold de-identified, aggregated data, but small counts at Prairie Gate (risk R-02) could identify people, so assess before concluding there is no risk.

Priya Raman (E-003), Chief Privacy Officer, leads every assessment and decides on notice for Kestrel, with legal counsel. Security supplies the facts; privacy applies the test.

read.heading: Internal escalation tiers
read.body:
In the table, CISO means Chief Information Security Officer and SOC means security operations centre.

| Tier | Who | Joins when | Decides |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Service desk, Grace Liu (E-005) | Every report | Log, prioritize, route security reports to tier 2 |
| 2 | Security analyst Sam Okafor (E-020) with Sentinel SOC Services (V-04) | Any security alert or report | Confirm an incident, set initial severity, first containment |
| 3 | CISO Daniel Osei (E-004) as incident commander | High or Critical severity, or any possible privacy breach | Containment strategy, declare a major incident |
| 4 | Marcus Bell (E-002), Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), Priya Raman (E-003) | Critical severity, clinical disruption or likely notification | Downtime, external notice, legal and ransom decisions |

Chloe Dubois (E-016) joins at any clinical disruption, and Kestrel's legal counsel and communications lead join at tier 4.

The finished matrix sets these Kestrel policy times, which are proposed targets, not law. For a Critical incident, Sam Okafor (E-020) tells Daniel Osei, Marcus Bell, Grace Liu, Chloe Dubois and Priya Raman within 15 minutes, and Daniel Osei tells Dr. Helen Marchetti within 1 hour. For High, the CISO and the system custodian (and Priya Raman if data is involved) hear within 1 hour; Medium within 4 hours; Low by the next business day. Any suspected privacy breach reaches the Privacy Office within the same shift, and Priya Raman completes the risk-of-harm assessment within 24 hours of the report.

Affiliates must report too, and many do not know it. Agency and vendor workers, such as ClearPath (V-03) nurses and Meridian (V-01) engineers, are affiliates under the HIA, yet only 48% of that group had completed privacy and security awareness training by 2026-09-30. Reporting routes belong in their onboarding.

read.heading: Communication roles during an incident
read.body:
Clear roles stop five people giving five different answers.

- Incident commander (E-004 or delegate): one voice, owns decisions, sets the update rhythm.
- Technical lead (E-020, with V-04 and Ahmed Haddad, E-017, for the network): runs containment and analysis.
- Scribe: records the timeline, decisions and evidence; this record feeds the post-incident review.
- Communications lead: drafts staff messages and media statements, which executives approve before release.
- Clinical liaisons (Dr. Sarah Whitford, E-007, for emergency care; Janelle Cardinal, E-008, for patient flow): translate technical status into clinical impact and back.
- Privacy lead (E-003): runs the breach assessment and writes the notices.
- Service desk (E-005): keeps users informed and the ticket current.

Plan for broken channels. If Email (A-013) or Clinical Paging and Secure Messaging (A-014) is affected, or possibly watched by the attacker, switch to a pre-agreed phone bridge and printed contact lists. Share incident details on a need-to-know basis, which protects both the investigation and the privacy of the people involved.

read.heading: Evidence handling and chain of custody
read.body:
An incident can start as an administrative matter and become criminal, civil or regulatory. The five investigation types are administrative, criminal, civil, regulatory and industry standards. Handle evidence from the start as if it may reach a court.

Collect in order of volatility, most fragile first: memory and running processes, network connections, temporary files, disk contents, logs held on other systems, then archives and backup media.

Make forensic copies. Take a bit-for-bit image through a write blocker, hash the original and the copy (for example with Secure Hash Algorithm 256, SHA-256), and analyze only the copy. Matching hashes prove the copy is exact.

Keep a chain of custody record for each item: description, hash, who collected it, when and where; then every transfer, with from whom, to whom, when, why and signatures; plus where it was stored and who accessed it. A gap lets someone argue the evidence was changed. Good evidence is authentic, complete, reliable and handled so it stays admissible.

Evidence can hold patient data. A CIS server image contains Restricted health information, so store it under Restricted handling and limit who can open it. When legal action or a regulator's investigation is likely, place a legal hold that suspends routine deletion of the related logs and mailboxes.

keyTerms.definition: The HIA breach test for health information. If loss or unauthorized access or disclosure creates a risk of harm to an individual, the custodian notifies the Commissioner, the Minister and the individuals.
The POPA test for non-health personal information: notice is required when a reasonable person would consider there is a real risk of significant harm. It is a higher bar than the HIA test.
Under the HIA, a person acting for a custodian, such as an employee, contractor, volunteer, student, agent or information manager. Affiliates must report breaches to the custodian.
The documented record of who collected each item of evidence, how it was identified and hashed, every transfer, and where it was stored, proving it was not altered.
Collecting the most short-lived evidence first: memory and running processes, then network state, temporary files, disk, remote logs and archives.
The single person who owns decisions during an incident, sets the update rhythm and speaks for the response, so teams do not act on conflicting instructions.

If yes, notify the affected staff, the Commissioner and the Minister responsible under the Act without unreasonable delay. examTips.tip: Domain 1, Security and Risk Management (legal, regulatory and compliance; investigation types): expect the right answer to involve legal counsel and the privacy officer before any external notice. Know the five investigation types: administrative, criminal, civil, regulatory and industry standards.

Domain 7, Security Operations (investigations): collect evidence in order of volatility, memory before disk, hash the original and the copy, and analyze only the copy. Any break in the chain of custody weakens admissibility.

pitfalls: Applying POPA's real risk of significant harm test to patient health information. Patient information falls under the HIA, whose test is the lower risk of harm.
Notifying only the Commissioner. The HIA also requires notice to the Minister responsible under the Act and to the affected individuals, in writing.
Analyzing the original disk instead of a hashed forensic copy, which breaks the chain of custody.
Coordinating an incident by email when email itself may be down or watched by the attacker.

check.q: Why is the HIA test easier to meet than the POPA test, and which applies to SEC-003?
check.a: The HIA asks whether there is a risk of harm to an individual; POPA asks whether a reasonable person would consider there is a real risk of significant harm, a higher bar. SEC-003 was unauthorized access on the CIS, which holds health information, so the HIA applies if patient records were accessed.

check.q: Under the HIA, whom must Kestrel notify, and how must individuals be told?
check.a: The Commissioner as soon as practicable, the Minister responsible under the Act, and the affected individuals, in writing. Kestrel may withhold notice to an individual if it could reasonably be expected to harm that person's mental or physical health, but must then tell the Commissioner.

check.q: What must a chain of custody record show?
check.a: What the item is and its hash, who collected it, when and where, then every transfer with from whom, to whom, when, why and signatures, plus where it was stored and who accessed it. Any gap lets someone argue the evidence was altered.

items.summary: Rank Kestrel's open vulnerabilities by risk to patient care, not by score alone: read CVSS correctly, weigh exploitability, asset tier and exposure, and plan patches, changes, compensating controls and risk acceptance for each finding.

read.heading: The vulnerability management cycle
read.body:
Vulnerability management is a loop, not a scan:

1. Discover: scanners, vendor advisories and findings from the security operations centre (SOC).
2. Assess: confirm the finding and score it.
3. Prioritize: decide what to fix first, using risk, not just the score.
4. Remediate or mitigate: patch, reconfigure, upgrade, replace, or add compensating controls.
5. Verify: rescan to prove the fix worked.
6. Report: trends, overdue items and exceptions to the owners.

The loop depends on the asset inventory you built in week 10. SEC-016 is a missing patch on A-021, a system that is not in khn_assets.csv. You cannot patch what you do not know you own, so the first fix for SEC-016 is to register the system and name an owner.

Kestrel's remediation policy sets due dates from detection: Critical 7 days, High 30, Medium 60, Low 90. On the as-of date, 2026-10-01, Kestrel has 10 unique vulnerability records. Two are remediated (SEC-011 and SEC-019), 8 are open, and 3 are past their due date: SEC-012, SEC-015 and SEC-017.

read.heading: CVSS: what the score means and what it does not
read.body:
The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) rates a vulnerability's technical severity from 0.0 to 10.0. Learn the bands:

| Score | Rating |
|---|---|
| 0.0 | None |
| 0.1 to 3.9 | Low |
| 4.0 to 6.9 | Medium |
| 7.0 to 8.9 | High |
| 9.0 to 10.0 | Critical |

The base score describes the flaw itself: how it is reached (network, adjacent network, local or physical access), how complex the attack is, what privileges and user action it needs, and the impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability. CVSS version 4.0 also has threat metrics (called temporal in version 3.1) and environmental metrics, so you can adjust for exploit activity and your own setting.

A base score is not a risk rating. It says nothing about whether your system is reachable, what it does for patients, or whether someone is already exploiting the flaw.

Check the data before you use it. Every score in khn_security_events.csv matches its severity band except one: SEC-017 is scored 11.5, which is impossible. Kestrel's rule DQ-05 says the record is not valid until it is rescored, but it stays on the open-risk list. A Critical remote code execution finding on PACS (the Picture Archiving and Communication System, A-004) must not vanish because its number is wrong. Sam Okafor (E-020) obtains the correct score; until then you treat it as Critical.

read.heading: Prioritizing by risk to patient care
read.body:
Weigh five things together: severity, exploitability (is there a public exploit, is it being used in attacks; published lists of known exploited vulnerabilities and exploit prediction scores help), asset criticality (tier and patient impact), exposure (internet-facing, reachable from user or vendor zones, or isolated), and how long it is overdue. Ages and overdue days below are calculated to 2026-10-01, and CIS is the Clinical Information System.

| Rank | Record and system | Score | Due, status | Why this rank |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | SEC-017 remote code execution, PACS (A-004), tier 2 | 11.5 invalid, treat as Critical | 2026-09-28, 3 days overdue | Lets an attacker run code; imaging supports clinical care |
| 2 | SEC-012 missing patch, CIS (A-001), tier 1 | 8.1 High | 2026-09-25, 6 days overdue | The most important clinical system, and its restores have failed twice |
| 3 | SEC-015 end-of-support software, Clinical Paging (A-014), tier 1 | 8.6 High | 2026-08-19, 43 days overdue | Support ended 2026-06-30, so no patch will come; isolate it |
| 4 | SEC-014 excessive permission, Identity Directory (A-007), tier 1 | 7.5 High | 2026-10-15, open 16 days | 12 systems depend on A-007 |
| 5 | SEC-016 missing patch, A-021, not in inventory | 6.5 Medium | 2026-11-07, open 23 days | Owner and exposure unknown |
| 6 | SEC-020 excessive permission, Clinical Data Warehouse (A-010), tier 2 | 5.4 Medium | 2026-11-28, open 2 days | Staging holds Restricted data |
| 7 | SEC-013 weak cipher, Email (A-013), tier 2 | 5.9 Medium | 2026-11-01, open 29 days | Email carries Confidential data |
| 8 | SEC-018 weak cipher, IT Service Management Platform (A-011), tier 2 | 3.7 Low | 2026-12-21, open 9 days | Lower impact |

You could argue SEC-015 belongs above SEC-012 because it is the most overdue. That is fine: the point of the plan is that you state the factors and can defend the order. The finished plan puts the CIS higher because its restores have failed twice, so an attack there is the hardest to recover from, and puts SEC-020 above SEC-013 although its score is lower, because warehouse staging holds Restricted data. Ranks 1 to 3 are all overdue and all need action this week.

read.heading: Patching clinical systems safely
read.body:
Patch management is a controlled process: keep an inventory and baseline; receive and assess the vendor patch; test in non-production; schedule a change window; take a backup and confirm the restore path; deploy in stages; verify with a rescan and a clinical check; document; and keep a rollback plan ready.

The CIS needs extra care. Both CIS restore tests failed: 9.0 hours and 13.5 hours against a 4-hour recovery time objective (RTO). If the SEC-012 patch damaged the database, recovery could take most of a day. So before patching: take a verified backup, confirm Meridian Clinical Systems' (V-01) rollback steps, choose a low-demand window and have downtime procedures ready.

Medical devices are different again. Their patches usually need the manufacturer's validation, so you protect them with segmentation and monitoring until a validated patch exists.

Link the plan to the schedule. Task 24, Remediate priority vulnerabilities, runs 7 working days from 2026-11-27 to 2026-12-07 with 2 days of float. SEC-012, SEC-015 and SEC-017 were already overdue on 2026-10-01, so waiting for task 24 is not acceptable. They go through Kestrel's operational change process now; task 24 covers the rest and the verification evidence.

read.heading: Change management and compensating controls
read.body:
Every fix to a production system is a change. ITIL's change practice (change control) and change management (CISSP) follow the same pattern: request, impact and risk assessment, approval by the right authority, scheduling, implementation, verification, review and records. Three types:

- Standard change: pre-approved, low risk and repeatable, such as routine workstation patches.
- Normal change: assessed and approved by the change authority, often a change advisory board (CAB).
- Emergency change: an urgent fix approved through a faster route and reviewed afterwards. An overdue Critical remote code execution such as SEC-017 qualifies.

Operational changes follow Kestrel's operational change process. The programme's change-control board, chaired by Marcus Bell (E-002), controls Beacon's baselines, not production patches.

A compensating control is an alternative that reduces the same risk when the primary control is not possible. SEC-015 is the case: Clinical Paging and Secure Messaging (A-014) is tier 1, its support ended on 2026-06-30 (93 days before the as-of date) and no patch will come. Until it is replaced:

- Move it to its own segment and allow only the flows it needs.
- Block internet access.
- Allow administration only from the management zone with multi-factor authentication.
- Ask the SOC to alert on any new outbound connection.
- Fund and date a replacement.

Then record a formal, time-bound risk acceptance by the business owner, Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), advised by Daniel Osei (E-004), with a review on 2026-12-17 (proposed). A compensating control must be documented, owned, tested and reviewed; it is never permanent.

keyTerms.definition: A 0.0 to 10.0 rating of a vulnerability's technical severity: Low 0.1 to 3.9, Medium 4.0 to 6.9, High 7.0 to 8.9, Critical 9.0 to 10.0. It is not a full risk rating.
How easily and how actively a flaw can be or is being used by attackers, for example whether a public exploit exists or attacks have been seen.
How much the business depends on a system. At Kestrel it is the tier in khn_assets.csv, with tier 1 for systems that patient care relies on.
An alternative control that reduces the same risk when the primary control cannot be applied. It must be documented, owned, tested and time-limited.
A change that must be made urgently, approved through a faster route and reviewed afterwards. It still needs authorization and records.
The date after which a vendor no longer issues fixes for a product. Unsupported systems must be replaced, isolated or covered by a formal risk acceptance.

Check every CVSS score against its band; record SEC-017's 11.5 as invalid, keep it open as Critical, and assign rescoring to Sam Okafor (E-020).
Rank the findings using severity, exploitability, tier, exposure and overdue days, and write one line that defends each rank.
For each finding, name the owner from khn_assets.csv, the fix and the change type (emergency, normal or standard); for SEC-012 add the backup and rollback check before patching the CIS.
Write the compensating controls and time-bound risk acceptance for SEC-015 on A-014, and the asset registration action for SEC-016 on A-021.

build.modelAnswer: SEC-015, Clinical Paging and Secure Messaging (A-014), High 8.6, end of support since 2026-06-30, due 2026-08-19, 43 days overdue on 2026-10-01. No patch is possible. Compensating controls: own segment with only the flows it needs; no internet; administration only from the management zone with multi-factor authentication; SOC alert on any new outbound connection. Replacement: business case to the sponsor. Risk acceptance: Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), advised by Daniel Osei (E-004), review on 2026-12-17 (proposed).

examTips.tip: Domain 7, Security Operations (patch and vulnerability management): CVSS measures severity, not risk. Given a lower-scored flaw on an exposed critical system and a higher-scored flaw on an isolated test server, the exposed critical system usually comes first.

Domain 2, Asset Security (asset retention, end of life and end of support): unsupported software cannot be patched. The answers that fit are replace, isolate with compensating controls, or formally accept the risk with an owner and an expiry date.
Domain 7, Security Operations (change management): an emergency change still needs authorization and documentation. It is approved faster and reviewed afterwards; it never skips control.

pitfalls: Ranking only by CVSS score, which ignores asset tier, exposure and whether an exploit exists.
Dropping SEC-017 from the list because its score is invalid. Fix the score and keep the risk visible.
Patching the CIS without a verified backup and rollback plan when its restores have failed twice.
Treating a compensating control as permanent. It needs an owner, a test and an end date.

check.q: Why is SEC-017 kept on the open-risk list even though its CVSS score of 11.5 is invalid?
check.a: CVSS scores run from 0.0 to 10.0, so 11.5 is a data error, not a reason to ignore the finding. The record describes a Critical remote code execution on PACS (A-004), 3 days past its 2026-09-28 due date. Kestrel keeps it visible as Critical, has E-020 rescore it, and leaves it out of score statistics until then.

check.q: What makes SEC-015 different from a missing-patch finding, and how should Kestrel respond?
check.a: It is end-of-support software on Clinical Paging (A-014), whose support ended 2026-06-30, so no vendor patch will come. Kestrel must replace the system and, until then, isolate, restrict and monitor it as compensating controls, with a time-bound risk acceptance by the business owner advised by the Chief Information Security Officer.

check.q: Why should the SEC-012 patch on the CIS be preceded by a backup and restore check?
check.a: If the patch damages the CIS, recovery may need a restore, and both CIS restore tests failed (9.0 and 13.5 hours against a 4-hour RTO). A verified backup, the vendor's rollback steps, a low-demand window and ready downtime procedures limit the harm if the patch goes wrong.

items.summary: Build the security-operations dashboard in Power BI: incidents by severity and category, mean times to detect, contain and recover that reconcile to 25.29, 1.93 and 28.33 hours, vulnerabilities by severity and age, control results, restore performance and awareness completion.

read.heading: What the dashboard must answer
read.body:
Daniel Osei (E-004), Sam Okafor (E-020) and Marcus Bell (E-002) need answers. Are we detecting, containing and recovering fast enough? Which vulnerabilities are overdue? Which controls fail? Can we restore the Clinical Information System (CIS)? Are people trained? Build three pages:

1. Incidents: counts by severity and category; mean time to detect (MTTD), mean time to contain (MTTC) and mean time to recover (MTTR).
2. Vulnerabilities: open findings by severity and age, and the overdue list.
3. Controls and recovery: control results, restore time against recovery time objective (RTO), and awareness by group.

Some measures are key performance indicators (KPIs), showing how a process performs; others are key risk indicators (KRIs), warning that risk is rising, such as overdue vulnerabilities and failed restores.

Security event data is Confidential in Kestrel's data dictionary. Apply the Confidential sensitivity label, publish to the Beacon Security Operations workspace, which only the security and executive group can reach, and give consumers the Viewer role or app access. Import mode suits these small files. It is schedule task 25: 4 working days from 2026-12-08, with 2 days of float.

read.heading: Prepare the data in Power Query
read.body:
Load three tables and give them model names: FactSecurityEvent from khn_security_events.csv, FactControlTest from khn_controls.csv and DimAsset from khn_assets.csv. Power Query renames the source columns to the names the measures use (record_type to RecordType, occurred_at to OccurredAt, remediation_due to RemediationDue and so on). Apply Kestrel's quality rules to the security events:

- Remove exact duplicates (DQ-01): SEC-005 appears twice; keep one copy.
- Fix casing (DQ-03): SEC-019's severity 'hIGH' becomes 'High'.
- Set types: the five timestamp columns as date/time, so blank times load as null; remediation_due as date; cvss_score as decimal number.
- Add SequenceValid (DQ-06), typed logical. It is false for SEC-008 and for every vulnerability.
- Null SEC-017's impossible CVSS score of 11.5 (DQ-05) but keep the row, so it still counts as open and overdue.
- Keep SEC-008, SEC-016 and SEC-017: flag them as evidence, never delete them.

Build the file work as a staging query named SecurityEventsStaging, with Enable load turned off:

```
let
    Source = Csv.Document(File.Contents("C:\Beacon\khn_security_events.csv"), [Delimiter = ",", Encoding = 65001, QuoteStyle = QuoteStyle.Csv]),
    Promoted = Table.PromoteHeaders(Source, [PromoteAllScalars = true]),
    Deduped = Table.Distinct(Promoted),
    Severity = Table.TransformColumns(Deduped, {{"severity", each Text.Proper(Text.Trim(_)), type text}}),
    Typed = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Severity, {{"occurred_at", type datetime}, {"opened_at", type datetime}, {"detected_at", type datetime}, {"contained_at", type datetime}, {"recovered_at", type datetime}, {"remediation_due", type date}, {"cvss_score", type number}}),
    #"Renamed Columns" = Table.RenameColumns(Typed, {{"record_id", "RecordID"}, {"record_type", "RecordType"}, {"occurred_at", "OccurredAt"}, {"opened_at", "OpenedAt"}, {"detected_at", "DetectedAt"}, {"contained_at", "ContainedAt"}, {"recovered_at", "RecoveredAt"}, {"severity", "Severity"}, {"category", "Category"}, {"asset_id", "AssetID"}, {"status", "Status"}, {"remediation_due", "RemediationDue"}, {"cvss_score", "CVSSScore"}}),
    WithSequence = Table.AddColumn(
        #"Renamed Columns",
        "SequenceValid",
        each [RecordType] = "Incident"
            and [OccurredAt] <= [DetectedAt]
            and [DetectedAt] <= [ContainedAt]
            and ([RecoveredAt] = null or [ContainedAt] <= [RecoveredAt]),
        type logical
    ),
    CvssChecked = Table.TransformColumns(WithSequence, {{"CVSSScore", each if _ <> null and (_ < 0 or _ > 10) then null else _, type nullable number}})
in
    CvssChecked
```

Change the path to your copy. The result has 20 rows: 10 incidents and 10 vulnerabilities. M stops evaluating an and as soon as one side is false, so vulnerability rows, which have no occurred time, return false at the first test.

read.heading: DimAsset, the Unknown member and the controls table
read.body:
DimAsset holds the 15 unique systems from khn_assets.csv plus one Unknown row, so a security record on an unregistered system stays visible (DQ-10):

```
let
    Source = Csv.Document(File.Contents("C:\Beacon\khn_assets.csv"), [Delimiter = ",", Encoding = 65001, QuoteStyle = QuoteStyle.Csv]),
    Promoted = Table.PromoteHeaders(Source, [PromoteAllScalars = true]),
    Deduped = Table.Distinct(Promoted),
    Kept = Table.SelectColumns(Deduped, {"asset_id", "system_name", "tier", "rto_target_hours"}),
    #"Renamed Columns" = Table.RenameColumns(Kept, {{"asset_id", "AssetID"}, {"system_name", "SystemName"}, {"tier", "Tier"}, {"rto_target_hours", "RTOTargetHours"}}),
    WithUnknown = Table.InsertRows(#"Renamed Columns", Table.RowCount(#"Renamed Columns"), {[AssetID = "Unknown", SystemName = "Unknown asset", Tier = null, RTOTargetHours = null]}),
    Typed = Table.TransformColumnTypes(WithUnknown, {{"AssetID", type text}, {"SystemName", type text}, {"Tier", Int64.Type}, {"RTOTargetHours", type number}})
in
    Typed
```

FactSecurityEvent then references the two queries above. It maps SEC-016's A-021 to Unknown and keeps the original value in SourceAssetID as evidence. It reads no file itself, because the Power Query privacy firewall can stop a query that both reads a data source and references another query; that is why the file work sits in the staging query.

```
let
    KnownAssets = List.Buffer(DimAsset[AssetID]),
    SourceAsset = Table.DuplicateColumn(SecurityEventsStaging, "AssetID", "SourceAssetID"),
    AssetMapped = Table.TransformColumns(SourceAsset, {{"AssetID", each if List.Contains(KnownAssets, _) then _ else "Unknown", type text}})
in
    AssetMapped
```

FactControlTest loads khn_controls.csv the same way: 13 rows, QuoteStyle.Csv kept because some results contain commas, dates and hours typed, and the columns renamed to ControlTestID, ControlName, AssetID, TestDate, Status, RestoreTestDate, RTOTargetHours, RestoreHours, TrainingGroup and TrainingCompletePct.

Relate DimAsset[AssetID] to both facts, one to many, single direction, so the dimension filters the facts. Leave FactControlTest unrelated to the date table: its restore tests go back to 2025, outside the date table's range.

read.heading: How MTTD, MTTC and MTTR are computed
read.body:
Kestrel defines the three times like this, in hours:

- MTTD: the mean of detected_at minus occurred_at.
- MTTC: the mean of contained_at minus detected_at.
- MTTR: the mean of recovered_at minus detected_at, over incidents that have recovered.

All three use only incidents with a possible sequence: occurred, then detected, then contained, then recovered, never going backwards. The approved results are MTTD 25.29 hours (n = 9), MTTC 1.93 hours (n = 9) and MTTR 28.33 hours (n = 8).

Why SEC-008 is excluded: it was contained at 13:10 on 2026-09-09 but detected at 14:30, which is impossible. Its containment time would be negative, and you cannot tell which timestamp is wrong, so all three durations are dropped. It still counts as an incident.

The SEC-005 duplicate is one lost-device incident recorded twice; counting both gives it double weight. MTTR has n = 8 because SEC-009 is still Contained, with no recovered_at.

Errors move the numbers (calculated from the CSV):

| Version | MTTD | MTTC | MTTR |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correct: duplicate removed, SEC-008 excluded | 25.29 (n 9) | 1.93 (n 9) | 28.33 (n 8) |
| Duplicate left in | 24.23 (n 10) | 1.82 (n 10) | 25.55 (n 9) |
| SEC-008 left in | 23.11 (n 10) | 1.60 (n 10) | 27.24 (n 9) |

Kestrel's MTTR runs from detection, not occurrence, and some organizations use MTTR for mean time to respond or repair, so print the definition on the card. Means are pulled by outliers: SEC-003 took 84.08 hours to detect and SEC-006 76.33, so the median time to detect is 14.67 hours. Show both.

read.heading: The DAX columns and measures
read.body:
Data Analysis Expressions (DAX) does the rest. SequenceValid already comes from Power Query, so you need only two calculated columns on FactSecurityEvent: a sort key for severity and the age of each vulnerability on the as-of date.

```
Severity Rank =
SWITCH ( FactSecurityEvent[Severity], "Critical", 1, "High", 2, "Medium", 3, "Low", 4 )

Age Days =
IF (
    FactSecurityEvent[RecordType] = "Vulnerability",
    DATEDIFF ( FactSecurityEvent[DetectedAt], DATE ( 2026, 10, 1 ), DAY )
)
```

Select the Severity column and set Sort by column to Severity Rank, so visuals show Critical, High, Medium, Low instead of alphabetical order. Then the measures. The first ten are the finished specification's; the last two serve the controls page.

```
As Of Date = DATE ( 2026, 10, 1 )

Incidents =
CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( FactSecurityEvent ), FactSecurityEvent[RecordType] = "Incident" )

MTTD Hours =
AVERAGEX (
    FILTER ( FactSecurityEvent, FactSecurityEvent[SequenceValid] = TRUE () ),
    DATEDIFF ( FactSecurityEvent[OccurredAt], FactSecurityEvent[DetectedAt], MINUTE ) / 60
)

MTTC Hours =
AVERAGEX (
    FILTER ( FactSecurityEvent, FactSecurityEvent[SequenceValid] = TRUE () ),
    DATEDIFF ( FactSecurityEvent[DetectedAt], FactSecurityEvent[ContainedAt], MINUTE ) / 60
)

MTTR Hours =
AVERAGEX (
    FILTER (
        FactSecurityEvent,
        FactSecurityEvent[SequenceValid] = TRUE ()
            && NOT ISBLANK ( FactSecurityEvent[RecoveredAt] )
    ),
    DATEDIFF ( FactSecurityEvent[DetectedAt], FactSecurityEvent[RecoveredAt], MINUTE ) / 60
)

Open Vulnerabilities =
CALCULATE (
    COUNTROWS ( FactSecurityEvent ),
    FactSecurityEvent[RecordType] = "Vulnerability",
    FactSecurityEvent[Status] = "Open"
)

Overdue Vulnerabilities =
VAR AsOf = [As Of Date]
RETURN
    CALCULATE ( [Open Vulnerabilities], FactSecurityEvent[RemediationDue] < AsOf )

Controls Passing % =
DIVIDE (
    CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( FactControlTest ), FactControlTest[Status] = "Pass" ),
    COUNTROWS ( FactControlTest )
)

Restore Tests Within RTO =
COUNTROWS (
    FILTER (
        FactControlTest,
        NOT ISBLANK ( FactControlTest[RestoreHours] )
            && FactControlTest[RestoreHours] <= FactControlTest[RTOTargetHours]
    )
)

Days Since Last CIS Restore Test =
DATEDIFF (
    CALCULATE ( MAX ( FactControlTest[RestoreTestDate] ), FactControlTest[AssetID] = "A-001" ),
    [As Of Date],
    DAY
)

Failed Controls =
CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( FactControlTest ), FactControlTest[Status] = "Fail" )

Awareness Completion % =
IF (
    HASONEVALUE ( FactControlTest[TrainingGroup] ),
    DIVIDE ( MAX ( FactControlTest[TrainingCompletePct] ), 100 )
)
```

AVERAGEX averages a duration that exists in no column, over only the rows you pass it. Writing the SequenceValid filter into each time measure means nobody can forget the exclusion, and because SequenceValid is false for every vulnerability, the time measures only ever see valid incidents. Awareness Completion % returns a value only for a single training group, because averaging percentages across groups of different sizes misleads. Beacon fixes the as-of date at 2026-10-01 so the expected values do not change from day to day; at go-live As Of Date becomes TODAY (). With no filters you should see 10 incidents, MTTD 25.29, MTTC 1.93 and MTTR 28.33 hours, 8 open and 3 overdue vulnerabilities, Controls Passing % of 30.8% (4 of 13), 1 restore test within its RTO (CT-003), 413 days since the last CIS restore test and 8 failed controls.

items.summary: Complete Kestrel's business impact analysis: rank clinical services by how harm grows over time, patient safety first, map each to its systems and dependencies from khn_assets.csv, propose the maximum tolerable downtime and set the recovery priority order.

read.heading: What a business impact analysis is for
read.body:
A business impact analysis (BIA) answers four questions. Which business functions matter most? How does harm grow over time when each one stops? What does each depend on? How fast must each come back? Its outputs, the maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) and a recovery priority order, drive every later decision: the recovery time objective (RTO), the recovery point objective (RPO), the disaster recovery plan and what you test.

Business continuity planning follows a sequence: set scope and get management support, run the BIA, choose recovery strategies, write the plans, test and train, then maintain. The BIA comes before strategy because you cannot choose a recovery site or a backup design until you know how long each function can be down.

In a hospital, start from clinical services, not systems. Clinicians lose emergency care or medication management, not a server. You map services to systems afterwards.

Beacon's schedule holds task 21, Complete business impact analysis and recovery targets: 5 working days, 2026-11-27 to 2026-12-03, on the critical path. Chloe Dubois (E-016), Business Continuity Lead, runs the workshops. Clinical owners rate the impacts and the sponsor, Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), approves the result. IT supplies facts; it does not decide how long care can run without a system.

read.heading: Impact categories, patient safety first
read.body:
Rate each service in a fixed order of categories so that money never outranks safety:

1. Patient safety: delayed treatment, medication errors, missed critical results, lost alerts.
2. Clinical operations: longer waits, fewer patients seen, beds blocked. Kestrel General Hospital (KGH) already has a median of 80.5 minutes from arrival to physician initial assessment in Q3 (July to September), so any outage there starts from a stretched baseline.
3. Legal, regulatory and privacy: duties under the Health Information Act (HIA), incomplete records, notification.
4. Financial: overtime, recovery costs, lost activity.
5. Reputation and trust: patients, staff and the board.

Rate each category at fixed time points (1, 4, 8, 24 and 72 hours) on a five-point scale: 1 minimal, 2 minor, 3 moderate, 4 major, 5 severe. The scale and the ratings are Beacon proposals that the clinical owners confirm in the workshop.

Rate impact assuming downtime procedures are running, because they will be. The question is not whether care stops when the Clinical Information System (CIS) goes down. It is how long paper and workarounds stay safe.

At Kestrel, MTD is the longest time a clinical service can run on downtime procedures before harm, patient safety first, becomes unacceptable. A service's rating at each time point is its highest category, and its MTD sits at or before the first time point rated 5 (severe); the owners agree the exact value. Qualitative ratings suit patient safety, where a dollar figure would mislead.

The depends_on column in khn_assets.csv gives the technical chain. The Identity Directory (A-007) is listed as a dependency of 12 of Kestrel's 15 systems. The CIS (A-001) is a dependency of four: the ED Tracking Board, Pharmacy, Bed Management and the Clinical Data Warehouse (A-010). So Pharmacy cannot be back before both the CIS and the directory are.

The column is not complete. Add the dependencies it misses:

- Access path: the Virtual Desktop Service (A-008) is how clinicians reach the CIS from shared workstations, yet A-001 lists only A-007. A CIS that runs but cannot be reached still stops care. SEC-004 hit A-008 on 2026-08-11 and normal service took 63.42 hours to return after detection.
- Restore path: every restore needs the Backup Platform (A-012), and A-012 depends on A-007 for sign-in. If the directory is encrypted, administrators need break-glass accounts that do not rely on it.
- Conflicting targets: A-012 has an 8-hour RTO, longer than the 4-hour CIS RTO that a restore relies on. Flag it for the owner, Marcus Bell (E-002).
- People and suppliers: Meridian Clinical Systems (V-01) for CIS recovery, NorthArc Cloud (V-02) for the backup platform, and staff to run downtime procedures.

read.heading: Recovery priority
read.body:
In the finished BIA the owners agreed these MTDs at the 2026-12-01 workshop: clinical communication 4 hours; emergency care, inpatient care and medication, and laboratory testing 8 hours; patient flow 24 hours; imaging 48 hours; analytics 120 hours. A system inherits the shortest MTD of the services it supports, so the CIS (A-001) and Pharmacy (A-005) get 8 hours and the Identity Directory (A-007) 4 hours.

Combine impact with dependencies to get the order. Recovery enablers come first, because nothing else can be restored without them. The RTO values are the targets recorded in khn_assets.csv.

1. Recovery enablers: Identity Directory (A-007, RTO 2 hours), the Backup Platform (A-012) and the management zone.
2. Clinical communication: Clinical Paging and Secure Messaging (A-014, RTO 2 hours).
3. The CIS (A-001) and its access path, the Virtual Desktop Service (A-008), both RTO 4 hours.
4. Systems that need the CIS or serve urgent care: ED Tracking Board (A-002), Pharmacy (A-005) and Laboratory (A-003), each RTO 4 hours.
5. Bed Management (A-006, RTO 8 hours).
6. Tier 2 support systems at 24 hours: PACS (A-004), the warehouse (A-010), IT Service Management (A-011) and Email (A-013). Email matters for coordination, so incident teams use the out-of-band channels until it returns.
7. Tier 3 at 72 hours: Power BI and the Beacon semantic model (A-009) and HR and Payroll (A-015).

The order is a proposal until the clinical owners and the sponsor sign it. It feeds the RTO and RPO recommendation, the disaster recovery runbooks and the ransomware playbook.

read.heading: Gaps the BIA exposes
read.body:
A good BIA surfaces problems nobody owned. Kestrel's data shows five:

- Pharmacy System (A-005) is tier 1 with no business owner, and its restore has never been tested (CT-004). The BIA cannot be signed until Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001) names an owner.
- Clinical Paging and Secure Messaging (A-014) passed its end of support on 2026-06-30 yet has a 2-hour RTO. An unsupported system with the shortest target is a contradiction to resolve.
- The CIS failed both restore tests: 9.0 hours and 13.5 hours against a 4-hour RTO, last tested 2025-08-14 (risk R-04, issue I-03).
- The Virtual Desktop Service took 63.42 hours to restore after SEC-004 against a 4-hour RTO.
- Only one of Kestrel's 8 tier 1 systems, the Identity Directory, has a passing restore test on record (CT-003, 1.5 hours against 2).

Each gap goes to the RAID log (risks, assumptions, issues and decisions) with an owner. For the project manager, the BIA is mostly stakeholder work: getting clinicians, IT and executives to agree ratings and priorities, and recording the decisions. For ITIL, it feeds service continuity management and the warranty of each clinical service. All four ITIL dimensions appear: people to run downtime, information and technology, partners and suppliers such as Meridian and NorthArc, and the value streams and processes of care.

A type of harm rated over time in the BIA. Kestrel rates patient safety first, then clinical operations, legal and privacy, financial and reputation.

items.summary: Set recovery targets for Kestrel's clinical systems with the rule that RTO plus WRT must not exceed MTD, test them against the real restore results (the CIS failed twice), choose backup types that can meet the RPO, and write a control-testing plan with population, sample and evidence.

read.heading: Four numbers and one rule
read.body:
- Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD): the business limit from the business impact analysis (BIA).
- Recovery time objective (RTO): the target time to get the system working again.
- Work recovery time (WRT): the time after the system is back to check data, enter records kept on paper during downtime, and resume normal work.
- Recovery point objective (RPO): the most data you can afford to lose, measured backward from the moment of disruption.

The rule: RTO + WRT must not exceed MTD. If clinicians need two hours after the system returns to catch up safely, the system must be back at least two hours before the MTD runs out.

Work it for the Clinical Information System (CIS, A-001). From khn_assets.csv: RTO 4 hours, RPO 1 hour. Agreed in the BIA workshop: WRT 2 hours and MTD 8 hours (the CIS inherits the 8-hour MTD of emergency care and inpatient care). On paper the design passes: 4 + 2 = 6, within 8.

Now test the design against evidence. The two real CIS restores took 9.0 hours and 13.5 hours. With the 2-hour WRT that is 11 and 15.5 hours, both beyond the 8-hour MTD. The last restore on its own took longer than the MTD. That is not a tuning issue; it is the patient-safety risk R-04, owned by Daniel Osei (E-004).

| System | RTO (data) | Restore test | WRT (agreed) | MTD (agreed) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CIS (A-001) | 4 h | 13.5 h (CT-002) | 2 h | 8 h | Fails |
| Identity Directory (A-007) | 2 h | 1.5 h (CT-003) | 0.5 h | 4 h | Passes: 1.5 + 0.5 = 2 |
| Pharmacy System (A-005) | 4 h | Never tested (CT-004) | 2 h | 8 h | Unknown |

read.heading: RPO and backup types
read.body:
An RPO of 1 hour means changes must be captured at least every hour. The CIS backup job is named BK-A001-DAILY. If that daily job is the only copy, Kestrel could lose up to a day of clinical documentation, far beyond the 1-hour RPO. Confirm with the custodian, Kevin Park (E-009), and NorthArc Cloud (V-02) whether transaction logs are backed up or replicated more often. The same question applies to the Identity Directory (BK-A007-DAILY) and Pharmacy (BK-A005-DAILY), both with a 1-hour RPO.

| Type | What it copies | What a restore needs | Archive bit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full | Everything | The one full backup | Cleared |
| Incremental | Changes since the last backup of any type | Last full plus every incremental since | Cleared |
| Differential | Changes since the last full | Last full plus the latest differential | Not cleared |

Incrementals are quick to take and slow to restore. Differentials grow each day until the next full but restore from only two sets. Transaction log backups and snapshots shrink the RPO between full backups. Replication keeps a second copy current within seconds, but it also copies corruption and encryption, so replication is not a backup.

Backup strategy: keep three copies on two different types of storage with one off-site, and make at least one copy immutable or offline so ransomware cannot change it. CT-005 passed on 2026-09-24: the latest CIS backup has an immutable copy at NorthArc in a Canadian region. Keeping data in Canada is a Kestrel contract requirement. Off-site methods you should know: electronic vaulting (backups sent off-site in batches), remote journaling (transaction logs sent off-site in near real time) and database shadowing (live copies kept on remote systems).

read.heading: What the restore tests prove
read.body:
| Test | System | Date | Result | RTO | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CT-001 | CIS (A-001) | 2025-03-20 | 9.0 h; database rebuild step ran long | 4 h | Fail |
| CT-002 | CIS (A-001) | 2025-08-14 | 13.5 h; restore runbook out of date | 4 h | Fail |
| CT-003 | Identity Directory (A-007) | 2026-09-10 | 1.5 h | 2 h | Pass |
| CT-004 | Pharmacy System (A-005) | None | No restore test on record | 4 h | Not tested |

Read the trend, not just the status. The CIS got slower between tests, from 9.0 to 13.5 hours, and the causes recorded are process problems you can fix: a long database rebuild step and an out-of-date runbook. By 2026-10-01, 413 days had passed since the last CIS test. Of Kestrel's 8 tier 1 systems, only the Identity Directory has a passing restore test; A-002, A-003, A-008, A-012 and A-014 have no restore test on record at all.

A successful backup job is not proof of recovery. Only a timed restore shows the data is complete, the runbook works and the target is reachable. Time the test from the moment recovery is declared to the moment the business owner signs that the system is usable, not from when the copy starts.

Recommendation for the CIS: rewrite and rehearse the runbook, work with Meridian Clinical Systems (V-01) to shorten the database rebuild, pre-stage the recovery servers, confirm hourly log backups for the RPO, and retest in schedule task 22, Test CIS restore and downtime procedures: 6 working days, 2026-12-04 to 2026-12-11, on the critical path. If 4 hours still cannot be met, a longer RTO is acceptable only if RTO + WRT still fits inside the MTD, and only as a decision by the sponsor, Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), advised by Daniel Osei (E-004).

read.heading: The control-testing plan: population, sample, evidence
read.body:
A control-testing plan proves controls work. In the table below, MFA means multi-factor authentication. For each key control, state the objective, owner, population, sample, test method, evidence, expected result, pass rule, remediation and retest date.

- Population: every instance the control should cover in the period.
- Sample: the items you test, chosen so the result represents the population. For a small, high-impact population, test everything.
- Method, from weakest to strongest evidence: inquiry (asking), observation (watching), inspection (examining records), re-performance (the tester does the control again).
- Evidence: dated, attributable, kept, such as restore logs with start and end times and the owner's sign-off.

| Control | Population | Sample | Evidence | Expected result and last finding |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 1 restore | 8 tier 1 systems | All 8: the CIS (CT-014) and Pharmacy (CT-015) in task 22, the other five in the 2027 calendar | Timed restore log, owner sign-off | Within RTO; 1 of 8 has a pass on record |
| Immutable backup copy (CT-005) | Tier 1 backup copies for November 2026 | The configuration once, plus 5 random days | NorthArc Cloud console export | Immutable copy in a Canadian region every day sampled; passed on 2026-09-24 |
| Privileged MFA | 6 enabled privileged accounts | All 6 | Directory export | 100% enrolled; CT-006 found 4 of 6 |
| Q3 access reviews | 18 reviews due by 2026-09-30 | All 18 | Review records | 100% with a decision; CT-007 found 12 of 18 |
| Leaver accounts disabled | Terminated or expired workers | All | HR list against directory | None enabled; CT-008 found 2 |
| Awareness training | 5 workforce groups | All 5 | Training records | 90% each; CT-009 to CT-013 show 3 groups below |

Keep the tester independent of the operator: Kevin Park (E-009) runs the backups, so the restore test is witnessed by Chloe Dubois (E-016) and signed by the business owner. Across all 13 control tests on file, 4 pass, 8 fail and 1 was never tested.

The most data loss the business accepts, measured backward from the disruption. A 1-hour RPO means changes must be captured at least hourly.
The time after systems return to verify data, enter paper downtime records and resume normal work. RTO plus WRT must not exceed MTD.
A backup of changes since the last backup of any type. Fast to take; a restore needs the last full plus every incremental since. Clears the archive bit.
A backup of changes since the last full backup. It grows daily; a restore needs the last full plus the latest differential. Does not clear the archive bit.
A backup copy that cannot be changed or deleted for a set period, even by administrators, so ransomware cannot encrypt or erase it.
The population is every instance a control should cover in the period; the sample is the items actually tested, chosen so the result represents the population.

Evidence check: last restore 13.5 h (CT-002, 2025-08-14); 13.5 + 2 = 15.5, nearly double the MTD. Status: not achievable today.
